questions.question: Announced in 2025, what type of engine is ISRO designing for Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**LOX-Methane engine**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation)** announced plans in **2025** to develop a new generation of launch vehicle (NGLV) equipped with **LOX-Methane engines**.
 
• The development of **LOX-Methane engines** is part of ISRO’s efforts to create more efficient, reusable, and environmentally friendly rocket propulsion systems for future space missions.
 
• **LOX-Methane engines** use **liquid oxygen (LOX)** as an oxidizer and **methane** as a fuel, which is a more sustainable and cleaner alternative compared to traditional fuels like hydrazine or RP-1 (kerosene).
 
• These engines are designed to cater to the increasing demand for launching heavy payloads into orbit, which aligns with ISRO’s vision for the next-generation space exploration and satellite deployment.
 
• The **LOX-Methane combination** also allows potential reuse of rockets, as methane burns cleanly and minimizes residue buildup within the engine, facilitating refurbishment for multiple launches.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **LOX-Methane Engines:**

 
 
• **Liquid Oxygen (LOX):** LOX is used as an oxidizer in rocket propulsion systems due to its high efficiency and ability to produce large thrust when combined with fuels.
 
• **Methane:** Methane is a clean-burning fuel that reduces engine residue, making it suitable for reusable rocket systems. It is also easier to store and handle compared to hydrogen.
 
• **Advantages:** LOX-Methane engines are more environmentally friendly, cost-effective, and offer higher efficiency for deep-space missions, as methane can be sourced from Martian soil for refueling purposes.
 
 
 
• **ISRO’s Next Generation Launch Vehicle (NGLV):**
 
 
• ISRO is focusing on developing the NGLV to replace its current workhorse launch vehicle, the GSLV Mk III, for enhanced payload capacity and greater reusability.
 
• **Applications:** NGLV is expected to support diverse missions, including launching communication satellites, interplanetary exploration, and large-scale space missions.
 
• **Reusable Design:** NGLV will incorporate reusable technology to reduce launch costs and increase competitiveness in the global space market.
 
 
 
• **Other Propulsion Systems:**
 
 
• **LOX-Kerosene Engines:** These engines are widely used in rockets such as SpaceX’s Falcon series but are less efficient and less environmentally friendly compared to LOX-Methane engines.
 
• **Hydrogen-Fueled Engines:** Hydrogen engines offer high efficiency but come with storage and handling challenges due to hydrogen’s cryogenic properties.
 
• **Cryogenic Solid Fuel Engines:** These engines are used for specific applications but lack the reusability and efficiency offered by LOX-Methane systems.
 
 
 
• **Global Context:**
 
 
• Space agencies like SpaceX and Blue Origin are already leveraging LOX-Methane engines for their reusable rocket programs, indicating the growing trend towards adopting this technology globally.
 
• ISRO’s development of LOX-Methane engines will align India with cutting-edge advancements in space propulsion systems and enhance its competitive edge in space exploration.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Why LOX-Methane?**

 
 
• **Clean Combustion:** Methane burns cleaner than kerosene and hydrogen, reducing engine maintenance and enabling reuse.
 
• **Storage Benefits:** Methane is easier to store as it does not need extremely low temperatures like hydrogen.
 
• **Space Exploration:** Methane can be produced on Mars using in-situ resource utilization, supporting long-term interplanetary missions.
 
• **Global Adoption:** Leading companies like SpaceX use LOX-Methane engines, showcasing their reliability and efficiency for modern space missions.
 
 
 
• **ISRO’s Contribution:**
 
 
• ISRO has consistently invested in advanced propulsion systems to enhance India’s capabilities in space exploration and satellite deployment.
 
• The NGLV project with LOX-Methane engines represents a significant step forward in making India self-reliant in next-gen space technology.

questions.question: Which of the following government bodies is responsible for disaster response and management at the national level in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**NDMA**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA)** is the **apex body** responsible for disaster management in India.
 
• It was **established under the Disaster Management Act, 2005**, which provides a legal framework for disaster preparedness, mitigation, and response at the national level.
 
• The NDMA is headed by the **Prime Minister of India**, who acts as the Chairperson.
 
• Its primary role is to formulate policies, plans, and guidelines for disaster management and coordinate with various ministries, departments, and state governments for implementation.
 
• NDMA conducts **disaster risk reduction and preparedness programs**, facilitates capacity building, and ensures the availability of funds for disaster response and recovery.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **SDRF (State Disaster Response Force):**

 
 
• SDRF is established by state governments to **handle disaster response at the state level**.
 
• It operates under the guidelines provided by NDMA but focuses on state-specific disaster management activities.
 
• It is responsible for immediate rescue and relief operations in case of disasters within the state.
 
 
 
• **IRDA (Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India):**
 
 
• IRDA is a statutory body formed under the **IRDA Act, 1999**.
 
• It regulates and promotes the insurance and reinsurance industry in India.
 
• Its primary focus is on protecting policyholders' interests rather than disaster management.
 
 
 
• **NITI Aayog:**
 
 
• NITI Aayog, established in **2015**, is the **policy think tank of the Government of India**.
 
• Its focus is on fostering cooperative federalism and developing long-term strategies for economic growth and development.
 
• It does not directly handle disaster management but may provide strategic inputs on disaster-related policies.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of the Disaster Management Act, 2005:**
 
 
• The Act envisages the creation of the NDMA at the national level, along with State Disaster Management Authorities (SDMAs) and District Disaster Management Authorities (DDMAs) at the state and district levels.
 
• It emphasizes a proactive approach to disaster preparedness, mitigation, and response.
 
• It mandates the creation of National Policy on Disaster Management and National Institute of Disaster Management (NIDM).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **NDMA's Vision:**

 
 
• To build a safe and disaster-resilient India by developing a culture of prevention, preparedness, and mitigation.
 
• To ensure a coordinated and prompt response during disasters.
 
 
 
• **Significant Initiatives by NDMA:**
 
 
• Implementation of the **National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project** (NCRMP).
 
• Promotion of Early Warning Systems for disasters like cyclones, earthquakes, and floods.
 
• Capacity building and training programs for disaster response teams.

questions.question: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) was established to formalise inflation targeting. How many members constitute India’s MPC?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**6**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** was established by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** in 2016 to formalize **inflation targeting** and strengthen India's monetary policy framework.
 
• The MPC is composed of a total of **6 members**. Out of these, **3 members are from the RBI**, including the Governor of RBI as the chairperson, and **3 are external members** appointed by the Government of India.
 
• The committee meets **4 times a year**, and its primary objective is to set the **policy interest rate (repo rate)** to achieve the inflation target set by the government.
 
• Each member of the MPC has one vote. In case of a tie, the RBI Governor has the **casting vote**.
 
• The inflation target is set under the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**, and the current target is **4% (+/- 2%)** for the period 2021–2026.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Composition of the MPC:**

 
 
• **RBI Members:** The Governor of RBI (Chairperson), the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, and one officer nominated by the RBI.
 
• **External Members:** Three external experts appointed by the Government of India for a term of **4 years**.
 
 
 
• **Objective of the MPC:**
 
 
• The main goal of the MPC is to achieve price stability while also considering the objectives of economic growth.
 
• The MPC is guided by the government’s inflation target, which is reviewed every **5 years**.
 
 
 
• **Inflation Targeting in India:**
 
 
• India adopted inflation targeting as part of its monetary policy framework in **2016**.
 
• The inflation target is currently set at **4%** with a permissible band of **+/- 2%**.
 
 
 
• **Decision-Making Process:**
 
 
• The MPC decides on the **repo rate**, which is the rate at which RBI lends money to commercial banks.
 
• Decisions are made by a **majority vote**, and the RBI Governor has the casting vote in case of a tie.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the MPC:**
 
 
• Ensures transparency and accountability in setting monetary policy.
 
• Strengthens the RBI’s ability to achieve its inflation-targeting goals.
 
• Contributes to maintaining macroeconomic stability in India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:**

 
 
• The MPC was formed under the provisions of the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**, following amendments made in **2016**.
 
• Before the MPC, monetary policy decisions were taken solely by the RBI Governor.
 
 
 
• **Global Context:**
 
 
• Inflation targeting is a widely adopted monetary policy approach globally, first implemented by **New Zealand** in **1990**.
 
• Countries like the **United States**, **United Kingdom**, and **Canada** also use inflation targeting frameworks.
 
 
 
• **Example of MPC Decision:**
 
 
• During the COVID-19 pandemic, the MPC reduced the repo rate to stimulate economic growth while keeping inflation within the target range.

questions.question: Which harmful social practice was banned in 1829 by Lord Bentinck during the British rule in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sati**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sati** was an ancient Hindu practice in India where a widow immolated herself on her husband's funeral pyre.
 
• Lord William Bentinck, the Governor-General of India, banned the practice of Sati in **1829** by implementing the Bengal Sati Regulation Act.
 
• The regulation declared Sati as illegal and punishable by law, marking a significant reform during British rule in India.
 
• The decision to abolish Sati was influenced by social reformers such as **Raja Ram Mohan Roy**, who strongly opposed this practice and advocated for women's rights.
 
• The abolition of Sati was a major step toward improving the status of women in India during the colonial period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Child Marriage:**

 
 
• Child marriage refers to the practice of marrying off individuals (usually girls) below the age of 18.
 
• The practice was prevalent in India and continues to be a challenge in some parts of the country, despite reforms and laws such as the **Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006**.
 
• This act prescribes punishment for those involved in promoting or conducting child marriages.
 
 
 
• **Polygamy:**
 
 
• Polygamy refers to the practice of having multiple spouses simultaneously.
 
• In India, polygamy is illegal under the **Hindu Marriage Act, 1955**, which applies to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs.
 
• However, personal laws for certain communities, such as Muslims, allow polygamy under specific conditions.
 
 
 
• **Dowry:**
 
 
• The dowry system involves the transfer of money, goods, or property from the bride's family to the groom's family during marriage.
 
• The **Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961**, was enacted to prohibit the practice of dowry and punish those demanding or accepting dowry.
 
• Despite legal prohibitions, the practice remains a social issue in India, leading to instances of dowry-related harassment and violence.
 
 
 
• **Sati and Social Reform:**
 
 
• The abolition of Sati was a landmark in Indian social reform, spearheaded by activists like **Raja Ram Mohan Roy**.
 
• The practice was deeply rooted in patriarchal and religious beliefs, which justified the immolation of widows as a form of loyalty.
 
• British intervention and Indian reformist movements played a crucial role in eradicating this inhumane practice.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Raja Ram Mohan Roy's Contribution:**

 
 
• **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** was a key figure in the fight against Sati. He argued against the practice, citing religious scriptures that did not mandate it.
 
• He founded the **Brahmo Samaj**, which advocated for reforms in Hindu society, including the abolition of Sati and promotion of education for women.
 
 
 
• **Legal Framework:**
 
 
• The abolition of Sati was formalized through the **Bengal Sati Regulation Act, 1829**, which made the practice illegal and punishable.
 
• Subsequent laws and reforms continued to address issues of gender inequality and oppressive practices against women in India.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Indian Society:**
 
 
• The abolition of Sati marked a significant step in the emancipation of women in India.
 
• It set a precedent for further reforms, including the promotion of women's education, property rights, and access to legal remedies.

questions.question: Which railway safety system did India begin implementing nationwide, covering 3,500 km in 2025 at a cost of ₹1,700 crore?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kavach Automatic Train Protection**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kavach Automatic Train Protection (ATP)** is an **indigenous railway safety system** developed by the Indian Railways to enhance train safety and prevent accidents such as collisions and derailments.
 
• The implementation of the **Kavach system** is a significant milestone in the Indian Railways' efforts to modernize its infrastructure and improve safety. By **2025**, the system is planned to cover a distance of **3,500 km** at a cost of **₹1,700 crore**.
 
• The Kavach system uses **state-of-the-art technologies** like signals passed at danger (SPAD), automatic braking in case of driver error, and real-time communication between the train and signaling systems to ensure the highest level of safety.
 
• It was successfully tested on **March 4, 2022**, with a demonstration attended by the **Union Minister of Railways, Ashwini Vaishnaw**, showcasing its effectiveness in preventing accidents.
 
• The Indian government aims to expand the Kavach system to cover the entire railway network, ensuring the safety of passengers and reducing risks associated with human errors in train operations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Features of Kavach System:**

 
 
• **Automatic Braking:** The Kavach system automatically applies brakes to prevent collisions in case the train overshoots a signal or encounters another train on the same track.
 
• **SPAD (Signals Passed at Danger):** It ensures that the train halts before passing a danger signal, thereby averting potential accidents.
 
• **Real-Time Communication:** The system allows real-time communication between trains and station signaling systems to provide updates on movement and track conditions.
 
• **Indigenous Development:** Kavach is a **Make in India initiative**, developed by Indian Railways, which ensures cost-effectiveness and promotes local manufacturing capabilities.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Kavach:**
 
 
• It aims to reduce human errors, which are a leading cause of train accidents in India.
 
• Kavach is expected to significantly enhance passenger safety and improve the efficiency of train operations on Indian railways.
 
• As part of the modernization drive, the Indian Railways plans to implement this system across its high-density routes and ensure safer and faster travel for passengers.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Options:**
 
 
• **Nationwide Railway Safety System:** This is a generic term and does not refer to any specific system implemented by Indian Railways.
 
• **Namo Bharat Signalling System:** No such system exists in Indian Railways under this name.
 
• **GPS-based Tracking System:** While GPS technology is used for tracking trains, it is not a comprehensive safety system like Kavach, which includes automatic braking and SPAD features.
 
 
 
• **Future Plans:**
 
 
• The Indian Railways has set a target to implement the Kavach system across **34,000 km of its network**, focusing on high-density routes.
 
• The initiative aligns with the government's vision of achieving high levels of safety and reliability in the railway sector.

questions.question: Which of the following texts is considered the earliest Tamil grammar work?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tolkappiyam**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Tolkappiyam** is considered the earliest Tamil grammar work and one of the oldest surviving texts in Tamil literature.
 
• It is attributed to the author **Tolkappiyar** and dates back to approximately **500 BCE** to **200 CE**, making it a foundational text for Tamil grammar and linguistics.
 
• The text is divided into three sections: **Ezhuttadhikaram** (phonology), **Soladhikaram** (morphology), and **Poruladhikaram** (semantics).
 
• Tolkappiyam not only addresses the grammar of the Tamil language but also delves into the social and cultural aspects of the Tamil-speaking population during ancient times.
 
• This ancient treatise has had a profound impact on Tamil linguistics and is regarded as a cornerstone for understanding the linguistic and cultural heritage of Tamil Nadu.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Silappadikaram:**

 
 
• Written by **Ilango Adigal**, Silappadikaram is one of the five great epics of Tamil literature and dates back to the **5th-6th century CE**.
 
• It is a narrative poem that tells the story of Kovalan and Kannagi, focusing on themes of love, betrayal, and justice.
 
• While it is a monumental work of Tamil literature, it is not a grammar text.
 
 
 
• **Manimekalai:**
 
 
• Manimekalai is another Tamil epic, written by **Sathanar**, and is considered the sequel to Silappadikaram.
 
• The story revolves around the life of Manimekalai, the daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi, and explores Buddhist philosophy and teachings.
 
• It is a religious and philosophical text rather than a grammar work.
 
 
 
• **Kural:**
 
 
• Also known as **Tirukkural**, this classical Tamil text was authored by **Thiruvalluvar** and is one of the most revered works in Tamil literature.
 
• It consists of **1,330 couplets** divided into three sections: **Aram** (virtue), **Porul** (wealth), and **Inbam** (love).
 
• Though it is regarded as a treatise on ethics and morality, it does not serve as a grammar text.

questions.question: What is the name of the principle which states that each point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that spread in all directions and form a new wavefront?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Huygens' Principle**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Huygens' Principle** states that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets, which spread out in all directions at the same speed as the wave. The new wavefront is formed by the envelope of these secondary wavelets.
 
• This principle was proposed by **Christiaan Huygens** in **1690** and serves as a foundational concept in wave theory and optics.
 
• Huygens' Principle is fundamental to understanding phenomena like **reflection, refraction, diffraction, and interference** of waves.
 
• The principle applies to all types of waves, including **light waves, sound waves, and water waves**, making it a universal concept in wave mechanics.
 
• It provides a clear explanation of the behavior of light as a wave, particularly when passing through media or around obstacles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Doppler's Principle:**

 
 
• Doppler's Principle, or Doppler Effect, explains the change in frequency or wavelength of a wave in relation to an observer moving relative to the wave source.
 
• It is commonly observed in sound waves and light waves, such as the change in pitch of a siren as it moves closer or farther away.
 
• This principle is widely used in applications like weather radar, astronomical observations, and medical imaging.
 
 
 
• **Fermat's Principle:**
 
 
• Fermat's Principle states that light follows the path that takes the least time when traveling from one point to another.
 
• It is a fundamental concept in geometrical optics and explains the behavior of light in phenomena like reflection and refraction.
 
• This principle is named after the French mathematician **Pierre de Fermat**.
 
 
 
• **Superposition Principle:**
 
 
• The Superposition Principle states that when two or more waves overlap, the resulting wave is the sum of the individual waves.
 
• This principle is key to understanding interference patterns and is applicable to all types of waves, including sound, light, and water waves.
 
• It explains phenomena such as constructive and destructive interference.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Huygens' Principle:**
 
 
• Huygens' Principle is used to derive laws of reflection and refraction.
 
• It helps explain the bending of light around obstacles, a phenomenon known as diffraction.
 
• The principle aids in understanding interference patterns, such as those observed in double-slit experiments.
 
• It is crucial in designing optical instruments like microscopes and telescopes.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Background:**

 
 
• Huygens' Principle was instrumental in the development of the wave theory of light, which later paved the way for modern optics.
 
• It was challenged by Newton's corpuscular theory but eventually gained acceptance due to its ability to explain phenomena like diffraction and interference.
 
 
 
• **Modern Implications:**
 
 
• The principle is used in computational methods like the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method for solving wave equations.
 
• It plays a critical role in fields such as acoustics, optics, and electromagnetism.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Public Order** is one of the subjects mentioned in the **State List** under the Seventh Schedule of the **Indian Constitution**. However, for Delhi, this subject falls under the purview of the **Central Government** and not the Delhi Legislative Assembly.
 
• The **Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991** and Articles **239AA** of the Indian Constitution specify the powers of the Delhi Legislative Assembly. Certain subjects like **Public Order, Police, and Land** are excluded from its jurisdiction.
 
• **Electricity** is under the control of the Delhi Legislative Assembly as per its legislative powers. It has the authority to legislate and manage electricity-related matters within its territory. *Hence, option 2 is incorrect.*
 
• **Education** falls under the purview of the Delhi Legislative Assembly, enabling it to make laws and administer policies related to schools, colleges, and universities in its jurisdiction. *Hence, option 3 is incorrect.*
 
• **Public Health** is another subject that the Delhi Legislative Assembly has authority over. It can manage healthcare services, hospitals, and sanitation within the National Capital Territory. *Hence, option 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Division of Powers in the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• The Indian Constitution divides subjects into three lists: **Union List, State List, and Concurrent List**, under the Seventh Schedule.
 
• Matters under the **Union List** are exclusively under the jurisdiction of the Central Government, such as defense, foreign affairs, and atomic energy.
 
• The **State List** includes subjects under the control of state governments, such as police, public health, and agriculture.
 
• The **Concurrent List** contains subjects where both the Central and State Governments can legislate, such as education and criminal law.
 
 
 
• **Special Status of Delhi:**
 
 
• Delhi is a **Union Territory** with a legislative assembly, governed under Article **239AA** of the Constitution.
 
• While the Delhi Legislative Assembly can make laws on subjects in the State List and Concurrent List, it cannot legislate on **Public Order, Police, and Land**, which are under the control of the Central Government.
 
• The Lieutenant Governor of Delhi acts as the representative of the President of India and has the authority over these excluded subjects.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Public Order:**
 
 
• Public Order refers to the maintenance of peace and order in society, ensuring safety and the rule of law.
 
• It covers matters related to crime prevention, riots, public disturbances, and enforcement of laws to maintain social harmony.
 
• In Delhi, the **Ministry of Home Affairs** oversees Public Order through the Delhi Police.
 
 
 
• **Other Legislative Powers of Delhi:**
 
 
• The Delhi Legislative Assembly can legislate on subjects such as **education, electricity, public health, and transport**.
 
• Examples include initiatives in improving public healthcare infrastructure and policies for ensuring quality education.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Article 239AA:**

 
 
• This article was inserted in the Constitution by the **69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991**.
 
• It provides the framework for the governance of the National Capital Territory of Delhi.
 
• It established a **Legislative Assembly** with the power to legislate on certain matters, excluding Public Order, Police, and Land.
 
 
 
• **Role of Lieutenant Governor:**
 
 
• The Lieutenant Governor is the **administrative head of Delhi** and represents the President of India.
 
• For matters outside the purview of the Delhi Legislative Assembly, the Lieutenant Governor exercises **executive powers**.

questions.question: What is the time limit to receive information from a public authority under the RTI Act?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2 (30 days)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005**, empowers citizens to seek information from public authorities to promote transparency and accountability in governance.
 
• Under the **RTI Act**, public authorities are required to respond to information requests within **30 days** from the date of receipt of the application. This is the general time limit.
 
• If the information sought concerns the life or liberty of a person, the RTI Act mandates that the information must be provided within **48 hours**.
 
• In cases where an applicant has filed an appeal with the First Appellate Authority, the authority must decide on the appeal within **30 days**, or in exceptional cases within **45 days**, with reasons for the delay recorded in writing.
 
• Failure to provide information within the stipulated time limit may result in penalties or disciplinary action against the Public Information Officer (PIO).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key Features of the RTI Act:**

 
 
• The **Right to Information Act, 2005**, was enacted by the Government of India to promote transparency and accountability in public authorities.
 
• It covers information on **government policies, decisions, and operations** to enable citizens to hold public authorities accountable.
 
• The Act applies to all levels of government—central, state, and local bodies—and includes public sector undertakings and institutions significantly funded by the government.
 
 
 
• **Exemptions Under RTI Act:**
 
 
• The RTI Act provides exemptions for certain types of information under **Section 8**, such as information affecting sovereignty, national security, or personal privacy.
 
• Information prohibited by court orders or legislative privileges is also exempt from disclosure.
 
• Commercially sensitive information and intellectual property are protected under specific clauses.
 
 
 
• **Role of Public Information Officers (PIOs):**
 
 
• PIOs are responsible for handling RTI applications and ensuring timely responses.
 
• They must provide the requested information or justify its exemption within the stipulated timeframe.
 
• Failure to comply can lead to monetary penalties and disciplinary actions.
 
 
 
• **RTI in India:**
 
 
• India enacted the RTI Act on **15 June 2005**, and it came into effect on **12 October 2005**.
 
• The RTI Act has been instrumental in exposing corruption and ensuring transparency in governance.
 
• Over the years, RTI has empowered citizens to access public records and demand accountability from authorities.
 
 
 
• **Global Perspective:**
 
 
• The concept of the right to information is recognized globally as a fundamental right under international law and is enshrined in Article 19 of the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR)**.
 
• Countries like **Sweden, USA, and UK** have similar legislation to enable access to government information.
 
• India’s RTI Act is considered one of the most progressive laws globally in ensuring transparent governance.

questions.question: Employment patterns during 1947-1991 showed limited diversification. Which sector employed the largest share of India’s workforce throughout this period?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Agriculture**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• During the period of **1947 to 1991**, India's employment structure showed limited diversification, with the majority of the workforce employed in the **agriculture sector**.
 
• **Agriculture** remained the backbone of India's economy throughout this period, contributing significantly to employment and being the primary source of livelihood for a large population.
 
• Despite the growth of other sectors like infrastructure, secondary, and services sectors, the pace of diversification was slow, and agriculture continued to dominate the workforce composition.
 
• Factors such as **limited industrialization**, the dominance of rural areas, and a lack of widespread urbanization contributed to the reliance on agriculture during this time.
 
• The **Green Revolution** in the 1960s did lead to some modernization in agriculture, but the employment structure still leaned heavily towards agricultural activities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Agriculture Sector:**

 
 
• In the post-independence era, agriculture was the primary source of employment, contributing to about **70% of the workforce** in 1947.
 
• The dominance of agriculture was due to the lack of industrial growth and infrastructural development, especially in rural areas.
 
• Major crops included **wheat, rice, pulses, and sugarcane**, which were cultivated extensively to meet food demands.
 
• The **Green Revolution** introduced modern farming practices, fertilizers, and high-yield crops, boosting agricultural productivity but maintaining agriculture's employment dominance.
 
 
 
• **Infrastructure Sector:**
 
 
• This sector primarily focused on **roads, railways, dams**, and other public works during the 1947-1991 period.
 
• Though important for economic development, it employed significantly fewer workers compared to agriculture.
 
 
 
• **Secondary Sector:**
 
 
• Industrialization was relatively slow, and the secondary sector (manufacturing and industries) contributed marginally to workforce employment during this period.
 
• India's **Five-Year Plans** attempted to promote industrial growth, but the results were limited in terms of creating large-scale employment.
 
 
 
• **Services Sector:**
 
 
• The services sector, including education, healthcare, and administrative work, showed growth during 1947-1991 but remained small compared to agriculture.
 
• Urbanization and modernization gradually increased its share of employment towards the later part of the period, but it did not surpass agriculture.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Green Revolution:**

 
 
• Introduced in the 1960s, this initiative aimed to increase agricultural productivity using modern techniques such as **high-yield variety seeds, irrigation, and fertilizers**.
 
• It helped India achieve **self-sufficiency in food production** but did not significantly alter the employment structure.
 
 
 
• **Employment Challenges:**
 
 
• Rural India faced issues like **low income, underemployment, and seasonal unemployment** despite the dominance of agriculture.
 
• The government's focus on promoting small-scale industries and cooperative movements aimed to address employment diversification but had limited success.
 
 
 
• **Urbanization:**
 
 
• Urbanization was slow during this period, which limited the growth of the industrial and services sectors.
 
• By 1991, India's urban population was only around **25%**, reflecting the dominance of rural employment in agriculture.

questions.question: What is the spatial resolution of the Bharat Forecasting System (BFS) launched in May 2025?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**6 kilometres**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Bharat Forecasting System (BFS)** launched in **May 2025** is a high-resolution weather forecasting model designed for India.
 
• The BFS has a spatial resolution of **6 kilometres**, which allows for detailed and accurate predictions of weather patterns across various regions in India.
 
• This advanced resolution enhances the ability to forecast localized weather events such as **thunderstorms, heavy rainfall, or cyclones**, thereby improving disaster preparedness.
 
• The BFS is part of India's ongoing efforts to modernize its meteorological capabilities, ensuring more precise data collection and prediction systems.
 
• The system is expected to benefit sectors such as **agriculture, transportation, disaster management**, and energy by providing timely and accurate weather forecasts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Spatial Resolution in Weather Forecasting Models:**

 
 
• Spatial resolution refers to the size of the grid used in weather prediction models. A resolution of **6 kilometres** means each grid cell covers an area of 6 km x 6 km.
 
• Higher resolutions, like 6 kilometres, allow for more localized and detailed weather predictions compared to coarser resolutions such as 12 or 10 kilometres.
 
• This is especially important in a geographically diverse country like India, where weather conditions can vary significantly over short distances.
 
 
 
• **Applications of BFS:**
 
 
• The Bharat Forecasting System will aid in **agricultural planning**, enabling farmers to make informed decisions regarding planting, irrigation, and harvesting.
 
• It will improve **disaster management** by providing accurate forecasts of cyclones, floods, and other extreme weather events.
 
• It is expected to support sectors like **aviation and shipping** by offering precise weather data crucial for navigation and safety.
 
• The BFS will also contribute to **renewable energy projects** by predicting weather conditions that affect solar and wind energy generation.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Spatial Resolutions:**
 
 
• **10 kilometres:** Typically used in older models, suitable for large-scale weather patterns but less effective for localized events.
 
• **3 kilometres:** Ultra-high resolution, often used for specific regions or research purposes but computationally intensive.
 
• **12 kilometres:** Standard resolution for global models, balancing computational efficiency and detail.
 
• **6 kilometres:** Ideal for regional forecasting, offering a balance between detail and computational efficiency.
 
 
 
• **India's Meteorological Advancements:**
 
 
• The BFS is part of India's initiative to leverage **advanced technology** for weather forecasting, enhancing the accuracy and reliability of predictions.
 
• It complements other systems like the **Doppler Weather Radar network**, satellite-based observations, and climate models.
 
• These advancements align with India's commitment to improving its **climate resilience** and disaster preparedness.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Bharat Forecasting System's Contribution:**

 
 
• It represents a significant upgrade in India's meteorological infrastructure, contributing to better **weather prediction accuracy**.
 
• The BFS supports India's goals under international agreements like the **Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction**.
 
• It helps integrate weather forecasting into various sectors, boosting **economic efficiency** and minimizing losses due to unforeseen weather events.

questions.question: What does GUI stand for in an operating system context?

__
 
• **Graphical User Interface (GUI)** is a type of user interface that allows users to interact with electronic devices using graphical elements such as windows, icons, buttons, and menus, instead of text-based commands.
 
• GUI was first introduced in the **1980s** with the advent of personal computers and has since become the standard interface for most modern operating systems.
 
• Operating systems such as **Windows, macOS, Linux (with desktop environments like GNOME, KDE), and Android** heavily rely on GUI for user interaction.
 
• A GUI provides a **visual and intuitive platform** for users to perform tasks such as opening files, navigating directories, and running applications, making technology more accessible to non-technical users.
 
• GUI uses a combination of input devices such as a **mouse, keyboard, or touch screen** to allow users to interact with the system in a visual and user-friendly manner.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key Features of GUI:**

 
 
• **Icons:** Visual representations of commands, files, or applications that allow users to interact with the software by clicking.
 
• **Windows:** Separate areas on the screen where individual tasks or applications run, enabling multitasking.
 
• **Menus:** Drop-down or pop-up lists offering various options or commands for user interaction.
 
• **Pointing Device:** Devices like a mouse or a touchpad are used to navigate and interact with the GUI.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of GUI:**
 
 
• **User-friendly:** Easier to use compared to Command-Line Interfaces (CLI), as users can interact visually.
 
• **Multitasking:** GUIs allow users to work on multiple applications simultaneously by using windows.
 
• **Accessibility:** Modern GUIs are designed to be accessible to people with disabilities, incorporating features like screen readers and magnifiers.
 
 
 
• **Disadvantages of GUI:**
 
 
• **Resource-intensive:** GUIs require more system resources such as memory and processing power compared to CLI.
 
• **Less Control:** Advanced users may find GUIs limiting compared to the flexibility of a CLI for complex tasks.
 
 
 
• **Examples of GUI-based Operating Systems:**
 
 
• **Microsoft Windows:** One of the most popular operating systems, known for its user-friendly GUI.
 
• **Apple macOS:** Known for its sleek and intuitive interface, popular among creative professionals.
 
• **Linux Desktop Environments:** Such as GNOME, KDE, and XFCE, which provide a GUI for Linux-based systems.
 
• **Android and iOS:** Mobile operating systems with touch-based GUIs for smartphones and tablets.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The first GUI was developed by **Xerox PARC (Palo Alto Research Center)** in the 1970s, which inspired future GUI developments.
 
• Apple's **Macintosh**, launched in **1984**, was the first commercially successful computer featuring a GUI.
 
• Microsoft introduced its GUI with **Windows 1.0** in **1985**, which evolved into the widely used Windows operating system today.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the legislative allocation of cooperative societies in the Constitution of India?

options.text: It is a subject in the State List
It falls under the Residuary (Union) List.
It is a subject in the Union List.
It is a subject in the Concurrent List.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It is a subject in the State List**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the **Constitution of India**, subjects are divided into three lists: the **Union List**, **State List**, and **Concurrent List**, as per the **Seventh Schedule**.
 
• **Cooperative societies** are specifically listed as Item 32 in the **State List**. Therefore, the state governments have the exclusive authority to legislate on this matter.
 
• The **97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011**, added a new part (Part IXB) to the Constitution, which deals with the working of cooperative societies. However, the legislative domain remains under the **State List**.
 
• The amendment also added the word “**cooperatives**” to Article 19(1)(c), ensuring that people have the right to form cooperative societies as part of their fundamental rights.
 
• **Statement 1:** "It is a subject in the State List" is correct, as cooperative societies fall under the exclusive legislative authority of the states.
 
• **Statement 2:** "It falls under the Residuary (Union) List" is incorrect because cooperative societies are explicitly mentioned in the State List, and residuary subjects are those not enumerated in any list.
 
• **Statement 3:** "It is a subject in the Union List" is incorrect, as cooperative societies are not included in the Union List.
 
• **Statement 4:** "It is a subject in the Concurrent List" is incorrect, as cooperative societies are not enumerated in the Concurrent List.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **State List:**

 
 
• It consists of **66 subjects** under the **Seventh Schedule** of the Constitution.
 
• State governments have exclusive legislative power on subjects listed in the State List, such as **police**, **public health**, **agriculture**, and **cooperative societies**.
 
 
 
• **97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011:**
 
 
• This amendment emphasized the importance of **cooperative societies** and their autonomy.
 
• It added **Part IXB** to the Constitution, laying down provisions for the effective functioning of cooperative societies.
 
• The amendment also inserted **Article 43B**, which directs states to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, and professional management of cooperative societies.
 
 
 
• **Union List:**
 
 
• The Union List consists of **97 subjects**, including matters of national importance like defense, foreign affairs, atomic energy, and railways.
 
• Only the Parliament has the exclusive power to legislate on subjects in the Union List.
 
 
 
• **Concurrent List:**
 
 
• The Concurrent List consists of **47 subjects**, where both the Union and State legislatures can legislate, such as criminal law, marriage, education, etc.
 
• In case of conflict between Union and State laws, the Union law prevails.
 
 
 
• **Residuary Powers:**
 
 
• Residuary subjects are those not enumerated in the Union, State, or Concurrent Lists.
 
• According to **Article 248**, the power to legislate on residuary subjects lies exclusively with the Parliament.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Cooperative Movement in India:**

 
 
• The cooperative movement in India began in the late **19th century** with the enactment of the **Cooperative Credit Societies Act, 1904**.
 
• Cooperatives play a significant role in various sectors like agriculture, banking, housing, and dairy production.
 
• Examples include **Amul** (dairy cooperative) and **IFFCO** (fertilizer cooperative).
 
 
 
• **Supreme Court Judgment:**
 
 
• In **2021**, the Supreme Court ruled that certain provisions of the **97th Constitutional Amendment** were unconstitutional as they encroached upon the domain of states.
 
• The judgment reaffirmed that cooperative societies primarily fall under the **State List**.
 
 
 
• **Role of Cooperative Societies:**
 
 
• Cooperative societies promote **economic welfare**, encourage **self-help**, and foster **mutual aid** among their members.
 
• They are pivotal in areas like rural credit, marketing of agricultural produce, and housing.

questions.question: What is the study of heredity and variation called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Genetics**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Genetics** is the branch of biology that studies **heredity** and **variation** in organisms.
 
• Heredity refers to the process by which traits and characteristics are passed down from **parents to their offspring** through genes.
 
• Variation is the differences in traits among individuals of the same species, which occur due to genetic and environmental factors.
 
• The term "Genetics" was coined by **William Bateson** in **1905**, who is regarded as one of the pioneers in the field.
 
• Genetics plays a vital role in understanding **inheritance patterns**, **genetic disorders**, **evolutionary biology**, and **biotechnology**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Evolution:**

 
 
• Evolution is the process through which organisms change over time due to **natural selection**, mutations, and genetic drift.
 
• It explains how species adapt to their environments and how new species emerge from existing ones.
 
• This concept was famously proposed by **Charles Darwin** in his book **"On the Origin of Species"** published in **1859**.
 
 
 
• **Mutation:**
 
 
• A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence of an organism's genome.
 
• Mutations can occur naturally or due to external factors like **radiation**, **chemical exposure**, or **errors in DNA replication**.
 
• They are a significant source of genetic variation, which is crucial for evolution.
 
 
 
• **Biology:**
 
 
• Biology is the study of living organisms, including their structure, function, growth, evolution, and distribution.
 
• It encompasses various subfields like **botany**, **zoology**, **ecology**, and **genetics**.
 
• The study of biology contributes to advancements in medicine, agriculture, conservation, and biotechnology.
 
 
 
• **Genetics in Application:**
 
 
• **Gregor Mendel**, known as the "Father of Genetics," conducted pioneering experiments on pea plants to understand heredity.
 
• Genetics is applied in fields like **medical research**, **genetic engineering**, **agriculture**, and **forensic science**.
 
• For example, genetically modified crops are produced using principles of genetics to enhance yield and resistance to pests.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Concepts in Genetics:**

 
 
• **DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid)** is the molecule that carries genetic information in most organisms.
 
• **Genes** are specific sequences of DNA that code for proteins and determine traits.
 
• **Chromosomes** are structures within cells that contain DNA. Humans have **23 pairs of chromosomes**.
 
• **Genetic Disorders** like **Sickle Cell Anemia** and **Cystic Fibrosis** are caused by mutations in specific genes.
 
• Advancements in **genomics** and **CRISPR technology** have revolutionized genetic research and therapy.

• The Svetambara sect of Jainism accepts these 45 Agamas as authentic and follows them as their religious texts.
 
• These texts contain philosophical concepts, ethical guidelines, rituals, cosmology, and spiritual practices to lead a disciplined and virtuous life.

questions.question: The opening of which of the following canals intensified British control over India’s foreign trade?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Suez Canal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Suez Canal**, connecting the **Mediterranean Sea** and the **Red Sea**, was opened in **1869**. It significantly shortened the maritime route between Europe and India, eliminating the need to circumnavigate the southern tip of Africa.
 
• The canal's opening allowed the **British Empire** to strengthen its control over trade routes to India, which was considered the "Jewel in the Crown" of the British Empire due to its economic and strategic importance.
 
• The Suez Canal facilitated quicker transportation of **goods, military supplies, and personnel**, which bolstered British dominance in global trade and improved the efficiency of their colonial administration in India.
 
• Since the canal reduced travel time and costs, it enhanced British access to Indian exports like **spices, textiles, and raw materials** and increased their ability to import British goods to India.
 
• The British government purchased a controlling interest in the canal in **1875**, further consolidating their influence over this crucial trade route.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Suez Canal:**

 
 
• The Suez Canal is an **artificial sea-level waterway** in Egypt that connects the **Mediterranean Sea** to the **Red Sea**.
 
• It spans approximately **193 km** and was officially opened in **November 1869**.
 
• The canal provides a direct maritime route between Europe and Asia and is among the most important waterways in global shipping.
 
• The British Empire's acquisition of shares in the Suez Canal in **1875** gave it a strategic advantage in controlling the route to India.
 
 
 
• **Conolly Canal:**
 
 
• The Conolly Canal is located in **Kerala, India**, and was constructed during the British era for irrigation and transportation purposes.
 
• While significant for local trade, it did not have a major impact on British control over India's foreign trade.
 
 
 
• **Buckingham Canal:**
 
 
• The Buckingham Canal is a **man-made waterway** in southern India, primarily used for irrigation and local transportation.
 
• It was constructed during British rule but was not connected to international trade routes like the Suez Canal.
 
 
 
• **Munak Canal:**
 
 
• The Munak Canal is an important irrigation canal in northern India.
 
• Although it facilitates agricultural activities, it is unrelated to India's foreign trade or British control.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Impact of the Suez Canal:**

 
 
• The canal significantly improved trade efficiency between Britain and its colonies, particularly India.
 
• Its strategic importance led to fierce geopolitical competition over its control, culminating in the British acquisition of shares in **1875**.
 
• The Suez Canal remains a critical trade route for global commerce today, handling about **12% of world trade**.
 
 
 
• **British Colonial Trade:**
 
 
• India was a major exporter of **cotton textiles, spices, and indigo** during British rule, and imports included machinery, manufactured goods, and British textiles.
 
• The Suez Canal played a crucial role in facilitating these trade flows.

questions.question: Which of the following Jain councils was held at Vallabhi (Gujarat) in 512 CE under the chairmanship of Devardhi Kshamasramana?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Second**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Second Jain Council** was held at **Vallabhi (Gujarat)** in **512 CE** under the chairmanship of **Devardhi Kshamasramana**.
 
• The purpose of the council was to **compile and preserve the Jain canonical texts**, which were at risk of being lost due to the declining oral tradition.
 
• During this council, the **Jain Agamas** (canonical texts) were written down and codified for the first time, ensuring the continuity of Jain teachings.
 
• This council marked a critical step in the **preservation of Jain literature**, as the teachings had previously been passed down orally.
 
• The council also sought to address disputes and ensure uniformity in Jain teachings, as the community was divided into two major sects: **Digambara** and **Shwetambara**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Jain Councils:**

 
 
• The Jain community held several councils to preserve and compile Jain teachings. These councils occurred at different times and locations throughout history.
 
• The **First Jain Council** was held at **Pataliputra** around the 4th century BCE under the patronage of King Chandragupta Maurya.
 
• The **Third Jain Council** focused on resolving sectarian disputes and clarifying the differences between the Digambara and Shwetambara sects.
 
• Each council played a significant role in ensuring the continuity and preservation of Jain spiritual texts and teachings.
 
 
 
• **Devardhi Kshamasramana:**
 
 
• He was a prominent Jain monk and the **leader of the Second Jain Council**.
 
• He took significant steps to preserve Jain teachings by compiling them into written texts, which were known as the **Agamas**.
 
• His efforts ensured the survival of Jain scriptures, which were under threat due to diminishing oral tradition.
 
 
 
• **Jain Agamas:**
 
 
• The Jain Agamas are the sacred texts of Jainism, containing teachings of the **Tirthankaras**.
 
• These texts were preserved through oral tradition until the Second Jain Council, when they were first written down.
 
• The Agamas consist of various categories, including **Angas**, **Upangas**, and **Chheda Sutras**, which provide guidelines for ethical living and spiritual practices.
 
 
 
• **Division of Jainism:**
 
 
• During the Second Jain Council, the Jain community was already divided into two sects: **Digambara** and **Shwetambara**.
 
• Digambara monks believe in complete renunciation, including the rejection of clothing, while Shwetambara monks wear white garments.
 
• The council aimed to address and reconcile differences between these sects, although the division persisted.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Significance:**

 
 
• The Second Jain Council was instrumental in preserving the oral tradition of Jain teachings by codifying them into written texts.
 
• It contributed to the **development and dissemination** of Jain philosophy and ethics.
 
• The council ensured that Jain doctrines remained accessible to future generations, safeguarding the religious and cultural heritage of Jainism.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Jain Literature:**
 
 
• The written compilation of Jain Agamas provided a structured framework for Jain teachings and practices.
 
• This initiative helped unify the community and maintain the authenticity of Jain scriptures.
 
• The texts became a vital source for understanding Jain philosophy, rituals, and way of life.
